opus-5.5.text:
I think if you want to rely entirely on real-robot data, a few conditions have to hold at the same time, and right now most of them don't.

The first is cost. Real-world teleoperation is expensive: you need the hardware, the operators, the venues, and the maintenance. For one hour of useful data you might spend several hours on setup, resets, and failed episodes. Pure real-data collection only makes sense once the cost per effective trajectory drops by orders of magnitude, so that you can reach the internet-scale volume that large models need, not thousands or tens of thousands of hours.

The second is the stability of the hardware itself. Robot bodies are still changing very fast: grippers, dexterous hands, sensors, kinematics. Data collected on one embodiment doesn't transfer cleanly to the next. If you bet everything on real data, you need the hardware to converge first. Otherwise you keep throwing away what you've collected each time the robot changes.

The third is diversity, which people often underestimate. It's not enough to repeat the same task in the same lab a million times. You need many different scenes, objects, lighting conditions, and failure cases, and especially long-tail situations. In the real world, setting up that diversity is extremely laborious. You can't easily rearrange a thousand kitchens.

The fourth is a closed loop of deployment. The most natural way to scale real data is the autonomous-driving path: robots are already deployed, doing useful work, and the data flows back for free. But that requires the robot to already be good enough that people want to use it. So there's a chicken-and-egg problem. You need data to get capable robots, and you need capable robots deployed to get data at scale.

So my view is that at this stage, real data is irreplaceable for the final alignment with physical reality, but it can't carry the whole burden. Simulation and synthetic data can provide the scale and diversity cheaply, especially for things like grasping and navigation, where the physics can be modeled reasonably well. Real data then fine-tunes and corrects. Maybe one day, when robots are deployed widely enough that the data flywheel spins on its own, relying purely on real data becomes realistic. But that day comes after robots are already useful, not before.

r001.rationale: It says hardware must “converge first” because data from one embodiment may not transfer when the robot changes.

r002.rationale: It describes high collection costs and says cost per trajectory must fall, but does not identify fully amortized robot manufacturing costs as a prerequisite.

r003.rationale: It discusses the expense of real-world data collection generally, but does not state that collection in China is less cheap than people commonly assume.

fable-5.1.text:
I think there are really three things that have to be in place before you can say, "okay, we'll just collect everything on real robots and skip simulation."

The first is that the hardware itself has to converge. Right now every lab, every company has a slightly different arm, different gripper, different camera placement. If the embodiment keeps changing, the data you collected last year is already partially obsolete. Real-robot data only becomes a compounding asset when the platform is stable enough that you can keep adding to the same pile for years. Look at what happened with autonomous driving — the sensor suite got standardized to a reasonable degree, and that's when fleet data started to really matter.

The second is scale of deployment. Collecting with a few dozen teleoperators in a lab is fundamentally different from having thousands of robots out in the world generating data as a byproduct of doing useful work. Teleoperation is expensive, it's slow, and the data distribution is narrow because it reflects what the operators chose to do in a controlled room. You need robots deployed in homes, factories, warehouses, where the long tail of situations shows up naturally. Until that deployment exists, I don't think real-world data alone can cover the diversity you need.

And the third is cost per useful sample. If you're honest about it, a lot of real-robot data today is low quality — repetitive, poorly labeled, with failures that nobody annotates. You need the collection pipeline to be cheap enough and the data to be rich enough that each additional hour actually moves the model. That involves better automatic labeling, better ways to recover from failures without a human stepping in, and some way of knowing what data you're missing.

So my view is that these are prerequisites that are coming, but we're not there yet. In the meantime, I think simulation and synthetic data remain essential, not as a replacement but as the thing that lets you reach the dexterity and generalization you need to deploy in the first place. Once robots are deployed at scale, the balance shifts naturally — the real data starts flowing, and you lean on simulation less. But you have to bootstrap that flywheel somehow, and I don't think pure real-robot collection can do that on its own.

r001.rationale: The response says robot hardware must converge and platforms must stay stable so data can accumulate on the same platform over time.

r002.rationale: It discusses the cost per useful sample, but does not identify fully amortized robot manufacturing costs as a prerequisite.

r003.rationale: It does not mention China or state that real-robot data collection there is less cheap than commonly assumed.

astra-6.text:
I think a few things have to be in place. First, the hardware has to be reliable enough that you can collect data consistently at scale. If every robot needs constant maintenance or someone standing next to it, collection becomes very expensive.

Second, you need an efficient way to get diverse, high-quality data. It’s not just about collecting more hours of the same task. You need different environments, objects, and failure cases, and a way to check whether that data is actually useful for learning.

And third, the learning system has to improve predictably as you add data. Otherwise, you can invest heavily in collection without knowing whether it will solve the bottleneck. So before relying entirely on real robots, I’d want to see that whole loop working: collection, training, evaluation, and then targeted collection to address the remaining failures.

r001.rationale: The response says the hardware must be reliable enough to collect data consistently at scale, which conveys relatively stable robot hardware as a prerequisite.

r002.rationale: It discusses collection expense and maintenance, but does not say robot manufacturing costs must be fully amortized.

r003.rationale: It does not mention China or claim that real-robot data collection there is less cheap than commonly assumed.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there are a few prerequisites. First, you need a reliable way to collect data at scale. The robot has to run consistently, and when something goes wrong, resetting it or recovering from a failure can’t require a researcher to step in every time.

Second, the data needs to be diverse. Collecting many hours of the same successful motion doesn’t necessarily give you a system that can handle new objects, environments, or unexpected situations. You need coverage of those variations, including failures and recovery.

And third, you need a learning pipeline that can actually benefit from that data. Can you turn each round of collection into a measurable improvement, then use the model’s weaknesses to guide the next round? If that loop works, relying entirely on real-robot data becomes much more plausible. Otherwise, simply adding more robots or collecting more hours may not solve the underlying problem.

r001.rationale: The response says the robot must run consistently and be recoverable without researcher intervention, conveying reliable, stable robot operation as a prerequisite.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention manufacturing costs or that they must be fully amortized.

r003.rationale: The response makes no claim about the cost of real-robot data collection in China or common assumptions about its cost.
